Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is a frog visibly present inside the toilet bowl?
node.criteria: Pass if the image clearly shows a frog within the toilet bowl; fail if the bowl is visible and no frog is inside it; unknown if the bowl or its contents cannot be assessed reliably.
node.binding: Assess the frog’s placement relative to the toilet bowl in the image, using the toilet in the input image as the reference. A frog elsewhere does not satisfy this check.

node_traces.evidence: A frog is clearly visible inside the toilet bowl in the edited image.

fulfillment: The node’s completion criterion is too permissive: it treats s1 passing as sufficient for complete fulfillment, and the traces merely repeat that a frog is inside the bowl without accounting for the other visible frogs on the toilet lid and floor. Preserve the requested-change and partial-progress distinctions, but make the decision assess the edited image against the full instruction and rubric: a frog in the bowl is clear progress, while additional frogs outside it may matter to whether the requested edit is complete. Do not infer the reference’s partial label as atomic ground truth; resolve the ambiguity in what “Put a frog in the toilet” requires, and ensure the node can distinguish partial from complete using image evidence rather than duplicated support claims. The traces are valid and queried, with no transport or dependency failure; their high confidence does not resolve this criterion ambiguity.
s2: The binding currently asks whether the edit was made, which lets a support node’s pass be mistaken for full completion. Keep this node evidence-only, but make its result explicitly report the visible progress and placement: the edited image shows a frog inside the bowl, plus frogs on the lid and floor; the source has no visible frogs. Do not treat those extra frogs as either proof of failure or an unstated requirement to remove them. Ensure downstream fulfillment applies the rubric’s distinction between any progress and complete fulfillment against the instruction, rather than equating this node’s pass or its dependency’s claim with “yes.” The traces are valid, queried, and high-confidence, so this is criterion/routing ambiguity, not a transport or dependency failure; confidence alone does not settle the aggregate label.
